passage: Okay Payal, you asked about video calls. Let me tell you about Tuesday. I am Indu, the designer. I was describing a banner, and I held my hands about this wide, a big rectangle, and said, "Something like this." Nobody reacted. Turned out my camera cropped everything below my chin. The client's video also froze right as she used her hands, so I have no idea what shape she meant. I laughed and said, "Sorry, I am waving invisible boxes." Then I typed 'A4 landscape' in the chat and shared my screen with a quick sketch. Everyone got it in seconds. Now I say the size in words first, gesture second.

qa.q: What did Indu type in the chat?
qa.a: She typed "A4 landscape" in the chat.

qa.q: Why did Indu laugh and say she was waving invisible boxes?
qa.a: She realised the camera cropped her hands so nobody could see the shape, and she wanted to lighten the awkward silence. The client's frozen video also meant she may have missed the client's gesture.

qa.q: What could Indu do next time a shape or size matters on a call?
qa.a: She could say the size in words, share her screen or make a quick sketch, as she did, and use gestures only as extra.

qa.q: How might the client have felt watching Indu's cropped video?
qa.a: The client may have felt unsure what Indu meant, since Indu's hands were invisible and the silence left both sides guessing.

grounding: Spoken monologue by a young professional whose gestures are cropped or delayed on video calls, solved by adding words and a shared sketch.

passage: I sat next to Chetan during the client call on Wednesday, so I saw both screens. Chetan held his hands wide, showing how large the packaging box should be, and the client on the screen just nodded blankly. Chetan looked pleased, but the client's face was frozen mid-nod for a second, so I could not tell if she understood. Then the client asked, "Sorry, how big?" Chetan looked surprised. I am Leela, and I leaned over and typed the measurement into the chat. The client wrote back, "Perfect, thank you." I think Chetan believed his hands were enough, but on camera they were cut off.

qa.q: Who typed the measurement into the chat?
qa.a: Leela typed the measurement into the chat.

qa.q: What did Chetan probably believe when the client nodded?
qa.a: He probably believed his hands had shown the size clearly and the client understood, and his pleased look fits that. The frozen nod meant the client might not have seen the shape.

qa.q: What could Chetan do on future calls to avoid this?
qa.a: He could add the measurement in words, type it in the chat or share a quick sketch.

qa.q: How might the client have felt when she asked "Sorry, how big?"
qa.a: She may have felt slightly awkward for interrupting, but relieved once the measurement was written in the chat.

grounding: Observer's account of a young professional's hand descriptions failing on camera, fixed by adding words in the chat.

passage:
Monday: On the video call, Eshaan held his hands about a foot apart. "The logo on the banner should be this big, and curved, like this," he said, tracing an arc in the air. His camera showed only his face and the top of his shoulders. Gopika, in Pune, nodded. "Got it."
Wednesday: Her draft arrived. The logo was tiny, tucked into a corner, and flat. Eshaan stared at it, confused and ready to type an irritated reply. Then it clicked: she had never seen his hands.
Friday: This time he didn't wave at the camera. He shared his screen, opened a blank page and sketched a banner with a big arched logo, then typed: "Logo width: about a third of the banner. Curved upwards." "Oh!" Gopika laughed. "On my side you just kept moving your shoulders." The next draft was exactly right.

qa.q: What did Eshaan type about the logo width?
qa.a: "Logo width: about a third of the banner. Curved upwards."

qa.q: What did Eshaan feel when he saw Wednesday's draft?
qa.a: Eshaan felt confused and irritated at first, then realised with some embarrassment that Gopika had never seen his hands on camera.

qa.q: What did Eshaan change on Friday, and why did it work?
qa.a: He shared his screen, sketched the banner and typed the size in words, so nothing depended on gestures the camera cropped.

qa.q: What was the Monday call like from Gopika's side?
qa.a: Gopika saw only Eshaan's face and moving shoulders, so she nodded along without the size or the curve, honestly believing she understood.

grounding: Shows hand descriptions being cropped on a video call and misread, and a shared sketch plus words removing the confusion.

passage: Abhinav, I saw you describing that bracket with your hands on the call just now, and the vendor's screen was frozen for half of it. Let me, Arohi, tell you a story. In my first year as a design engineer, the internet at our Shillong office was terrible. I was explaining a pipe joint to the workshop in Coimbatore: "It bends like this, then narrows like this," my hands doing all the work. The video kept freezing and jumping. The foreman nodded politely. Two weeks later a crate arrived with forty joints bent the wrong way. I remember sitting on that crate feeling sick. After that I never described a shape with my hands alone on a call. I'd hold a sketch up to the camera, send a photo of it in the chat, and ask them to tell me back what they understood. Try it this afternoon.

qa.q: How many joints arrived bent the wrong way?
qa.a: Forty joints.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel sitting on the crate?
qa.a: Arohi felt sick with dismay and probably some guilt, realising the frozen video had hidden the hand descriptions the foreman needed.

qa.q: What change did Arohi make after that turning point?
qa.a: Arohi stopped relying on hand shapes alone, held up a sketch, sent a photo of it in the chat and asked the workshop to repeat back what they understood.

qa.q: How might the foreman in Coimbatore have experienced that call?
qa.a: The foreman likely saw a jumping, frozen picture and caught only fragments, but nodded politely, perhaps not wanting to seem slow or to question the engineer.

grounding: An elder recalls hand descriptions being lost on a laggy video call and learning to add sketches and ask for a read-back.

passage: Hafsa's laptop camera had died that morning, so she joined the call on her phone, propped against a mug, with nine percent battery. Arnab, the new intern, was setting up the conference hall for Saturday's workshop and needed the seating plan. "Tables in a horseshoe, like this," Hafsa said, curving both hands into a U. On Arnab's screen, the phone showed only her forehead and the ceiling fan. "Like... a circle?" he asked. "No, open at the front. Like this!" She made the U bigger. The picture froze, then jumped. Arnab looked more lost. Seven percent. Hafsa stopped gesturing. She grabbed a sticky note, drew a U with little squares for tables and an arrow marked "stage", and held it right up to the camera. Then she typed in the chat: "U shape, open end facing the stage, 12 tables." "Oh, a horseshoe!" Arnab said. "Got it." The screen went black.

qa.q: How many tables did Hafsa type in the chat?
qa.a: 12 tables.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when he asked 'Like... a circle?'
qa.a: Arnab felt confused and unsure, because the phone showed only Hafsa's forehead and the ceiling fan, not her hands.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do that finally worked under time pressure?
qa.a: She stopped gesturing, drew the layout on a sticky note and held it to the camera, then typed the shape and table count in the chat.

qa.q: What would have changed if Hafsa's battery had died before she typed the message?
qa.a: Arnab might have set up the wrong layout, since the frozen gestures alone never showed him the horseshoe shape.

grounding: Shows hand shapes going unseen on a cropped, laggy call and a quick sketch plus typed words clearing up the confusion.

passage:
From his rented flat in Indiranagar, Saurabh held his hands apart in front of the laptop. "The new display stand should be about this wide, okay? Not bigger."
On the other end, Nikita squinted. Her screen showed Saurabh's face, a ceiling fan and the tips of two fingers at the very edges of the frame. The video stuttered, and his hands froze mid-air.
"About... how wide?" she asked. "I can see one thumb."
"This wide!" He spread them again, further this time, forgetting the camera.
Nikita wrote down "large" and frowned. The shop's corner was tiny.
Two days later the carpenter's drawing arrived: a stand nearly two metres across. Saurabh groaned. On the next call he typed "90 cm" in the chat, then held a quick pencil sketch up to the camera.
Nikita laughed. "Now that I can see."

qa.q: What could Nikita see of Saurabh's hands?
qa.a: She could see the tips of two fingers at the very edges of the frame.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling as she wrote down "large"?
qa.a: Nikita felt unsure and a bit uneasy, since she couldn't really see the gesture and knew the shop's corner was tiny.

qa.q: What fixed the confusion on the next call?
qa.a: Typing the exact size, 90 cm, in the chat and holding up a quick sketch, so the size no longer depended on cropped hands.

qa.q: What would have changed if they had met in the shop?
qa.a: Nikita could have seen the full width of his hands against the real corner, so the size would likely have been clear from the start.

grounding: On a video call, hand descriptions get cropped or frozen and are misread, so typed words and a sketch reduce confusion.
